t.jartepa ii temple@39.5,67.3:
The Zarafshan valley is the green artery of central Uzbekistan, carrying meltwater from the mountains of Tajikistan west past Samarkand and Bukhara into the desert. South of Samarkand, the land rises into the foothills of the Zarafshan range, and it is here, near Urgut and close to the Tajik border, that the Jartepa site lies, with remains of a temple from the Sogdian era.

The Sogdians were the great merchants of the Silk Road, an Iranian people whose language and trading networks stretched from Persia to China in the centuries before the Arab conquest. Their cities and temples dotted the valley, and Samarkand, then called Maracanda, was their most important centre. Temple sites like Jartepa show the religious life of the time, which mixed Zoroastrian elements with local cults. Across the border near Panjakent, the excavated Sogdian town has yielded famous wall paintings. The Jartepa site is an archaeological location, so expect excavated walls and foundations rather than a restored monument.

Urgut, about fourteen kilometres away, is a lively market town known for its huge bazaar, particularly its Sunday market, where you can find textiles, embroidered suzani and all manner of goods. The town sits at the foot of the mountains, with plane trees and a famous old chinar grove, and roads lead up into the hills toward walnut forests and mountain villages.

Riding in Uzbekistan requires preparation. Fuel can be a challenge: many vehicles run on compressed natural gas, petrol stations may only stock low-octane fuel, and supplies can be patchy outside cities, so carry extra and fill up whenever you see good fuel. Check entry rules for bringing your own vehicle. Roads range from good highways to badly broken rural tracks, and police checkpoints are common. The roads into the mountains south of Samarkand are scenic and quiet but often rough, with steep sections.

Samarkand itself, with the Registan, Shah-i-Zinda and Gur-e-Amir, is the obvious base, with good accommodation and food. Plov, the national rice dish, is best at lunchtime, and the bread of Samarkand is famous throughout the country. Spring and autumn are ideal; summer is very hot and winter can be cold.
t.suleimantepa@39.4,67.2:
Urgut is only a few kilometres from here, and if you ride into town on a market day you will understand quickly why the Silk Road needed places like this. The bazaar in Urgut is one of the biggest in Uzbekistan, sprawling, loud and full of everything from suzani embroidery and old coins to cattle and car parts. Suleimantepa, a low mound just outside, is one of the archaeological sites recognised as part of the Zarafshan valley corridor of the Silk Roads, the chain of settlements, forts and caravan stops along the river that fed Samarkand and Bukhara.

A tepa in this part of the world is a hill made by people: layer upon layer of mud-brick houses, walls and rubbish built on top of each other over centuries until a town becomes a mound. There is not much to look at in the way of standing walls, so come with imagination and patience. Stand on top, look north over the irrigated fields toward the Zarafshan, then south to the hills, and picture caravans trading silk, glass, horses and ideas between China, Persia and the steppe. Sogdian merchants from this valley were the great middlemen of that trade for centuries.

The riding around Urgut is a pleasant change from the flat cotton plains. The town sits where the valley meets the foothills of the Zarafshan range, and roads climb south into the mountains toward villages with walnut and apricot orchards and fast cold streams. Surfaces vary from fresh tarmac to broken patches and dust, and you share the road with Damas minivans, donkey carts and drivers whose relationship with lanes is flexible. Summer afternoons are hot, often well over thirty-five degrees, so the cool mornings of spring and autumn are better, when the orchards are blossoming or heavy with fruit. Police checkpoints are common in Uzbekistan; keep your documents to hand and stay calm and friendly.

Urgut has fuel, food and everything a rider needs, though fuel supply in Uzbekistan has historically been patchy and many vehicles run on gas, so fill up when you see petrol. Do not leave town without seeing the Chor-Chinor grove, a garden of enormous ancient plane trees around a spring and a mosque, where families picnic in the shade and the air feels ten degrees cooler. Samarkand is roughly an hour away, close enough to combine with Registan and Shah-i-Zinda in one day, but Urgut deserves its own slow afternoon with tea, fresh non bread and a plate of plov.
t.shahristoni zoli zar@37.6,69.5:
Down in the far south of Tajikistan, in Khatlon province, the land flattens into the wide floodplain of the Panj, the river that forms the border with Afghanistan. The site named Shahristoni Zoli Zar lies in this country, some eighteen kilometres from Farkhor, and it is one of many ancient settlement mounds scattered across the region. Southern Tajikistan was part of ancient Bactria, later the heartland of the Kushan empire, and the fields here have yielded Buddhist and early Islamic remains. A shahriston, in the old local sense, was the inner walled town, and the name suggests that this mound once held a proper urban core.

Honesty matters here: few detailed accounts of this particular site are published in English, and you should not expect signposts, fences or a visitor centre. What you get is a low tell rising out of cotton fields and irrigation channels, with the mountains of northern Afghanistan hazy on the southern horizon. Ask locally before walking on it; farmers will usually point the way and may offer tea.

Riding in Khatlon is hot, flat and dusty for much of the year. Summer temperatures climb well past forty degrees, so ride early, carry plenty of water and plan rest in the shade through the middle of the day. Roads between the district towns are mostly paved, with potholes, animals, slow trucks and the occasional checkpoint near the border. Keep your passport and permits handy, be polite at checks, and do not photograph border installations.

Farkhor is a district town of around twenty thousand people with fuel, a bazaar and simple chaikhanas serving plov, shashlik and fresh flatbread. Spring, when the irrigated fields are green and the air still mild, is the loveliest season, and autumn brings the cotton harvest. This is not a polished tourist trail. It is a ride through one of Central Asia's oldest farmed landscapes, along a river that has been a frontier for empires since Alexander, and the reward is the feeling of being somewhere very few travellers bother to stop.
t.proto urban site of sarazm@39.5,67.5:
Five thousand years ago, in the fertile Zeravshan valley of what is now north-western Tajikistan, people built a settlement of mud-brick houses, temples and workshops that became one of the earliest towns in Central Asia. Sarazm, near Panjakent and right next to the Uzbek border, was a centre of metal working, trading copper, tin and turquoise with places as far away as Iran, Afghanistan and India. Inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2010, the site has revealed burials with jewellery, including the richly adorned grave of a woman known as the Princess of Sarazm.

The excavated areas are protected under shelters, and a small museum displays some finds. The valley around is green and fertile, with orchards, vineyards and fields, framed by the Zeravshan and Turkestan mountains. In late spring the apricot and mulberry trees are heavy with fruit, and children sell it by the roadside in plastic bags.

Panjakent, thirteen kilometres away, is the main town of the area, with fuel, a lively bazaar, and simple hotels and restaurants. On the edge of town lie the ruins of ancient Panjakent, a Sogdian city of the fifth to eighth centuries, with remains of houses, temples and a citadel. Its wall paintings, now mostly in the Hermitage in St Petersburg and the Rudaki museum in Panjakent, show scenes of Sogdian life, myth and religion. The poet Rudaki, considered the father of Persian poetry, is buried nearby.

The Fann mountains, south of Panjakent, are one of the most beautiful ranges in Central Asia, with turquoise lakes, including the Seven Lakes, Haft Kul, reached by a rough road up the Shing valley. The roads are mostly unpaved and challenging, with steep climbs and river crossings. The main road east to Ayni and Dushanbe follows the Zeravshan valley, with tunnels and mountain passes. Spring and autumn are ideal, while summer can be hot in the valley. Carry cash, a good map and extra fuel for mountain excursions.
t.kafirkala settlement@39.6,67.0:
A few kilometres south of Samarkand, on a mound beside an old irrigation canal, lie the ruins of Kafirkala, a fortified settlement that was an important centre of the Sogdian civilisation before the Arab conquest in the eighth century. The name means fortress of the infidels, given later by Muslim inhabitants. Excavations have revealed a citadel with walls, a palace and remains that tell of the last days of the Sogdian rulers before the city was burned.

Sogdiana was a land of merchants who dominated trade along the Silk Road between China and the West, and their language was the lingua franca of Central Asian commerce for centuries. Samarkand, then called Marakanda, was their great city, and its ruins at Afrasiyab, on the northern edge of modern Samarkand, include famous wall paintings of foreign embassies. Kafirkala, on the southern approach, controlled the canals that brought water from the Zeravshan river to the fields.

Riding around Samarkand is a mix of city traffic and open country roads. The city itself is busy, with wide avenues, roundabouts and a lot of taxis and minibuses, and driving can be chaotic. Outside, the roads cross fertile farmland irrigated by canals, with cotton fields, orchards and vineyards, and the mountains of the Zeravshan range rise to the south. The road south from Samarkand towards Shakhrisabz crosses the Takhtakaracha pass, a winding climb with fine views. Summers are very hot and dry; spring and autumn are ideal.

Samarkand, eleven kilometres away, has fuel and all services, though fuel quality and availability can vary in Uzbekistan, and many vehicles run on compressed gas, so petrol stations can be scarce; fill up when you can. The city's monuments, the Registan, the Gur-e-Amir and the Bibi-Khanym mosque, are among the most magnificent in the Islamic world. Uzbek food is a treat: plov, samsa and fresh bread from the clay ovens. Kafirkala is quiet and rarely visited, a contrast to the crowds in the city.
t.halevard@37.6,68.6:
Southern Tajikistan is a land of wide river valleys and dry hills, where the Vakhsh and the Panj rivers flow towards the Amu Darya, the Oxus of the ancients, on the border with Afghanistan. Near the town of Kolkhozobod, known today by its newer name, lies Halevard, an archaeological site in the fertile Vakhsh valley. This region was part of ancient Bactria, a land of cities and fortresses that flourished under the Persians, the Greeks who followed Alexander the Great, and the Kushans.

The Vakhsh valley holds many ancient sites, and the most famous is Takhti-Sangin, on the Amu Darya, a temple where archaeologists found treasures linked to the Oxus Treasure, a collection of gold and silver objects now in the British Museum. The Tigrovaya Balka nature reserve, at the confluence of the Vakhsh and the Panj, protects tugay forests, dense riverine woodlands of poplar and tamarisk, which were once home to the Caspian tiger, now extinct. The reserve is still home to Bukhara deer and many birds.

Riding in Tajikistan is an adventure. The roads in the south are mostly paved but can be rough, with potholes, and traffic includes old cars, trucks and livestock. The heat in summer is intense, often above forty degrees, so ride early in the morning. Police checkpoints are common, and the border area with Afghanistan has restrictions, so check current advice and carry your documents. The Pamir Highway, one of the great motorcycle roads of the world, starts further east, and many riders pass through the south on their way there.

Kolkhozobod, about a kilometre away, is a town with fuel and basic services, and Dushanbe, the capital, is a few hours' ride to the north. Fuel quality can vary, so fill up at reliable stations. Tajik food includes plov, rice with meat and carrots, shashlik and fresh bread from clay ovens, and green tea is served everywhere. Tajik hospitality is warm, and travellers are often invited into homes. Riding through the Vakhsh valley in the evening, with the cotton fields glowing and the mountains in the distance, is beautiful.
t.manzaratepa@37.8,69.6:
Tepa means mound, and in southern Tajikistan the plains are dotted with them: hills built up over centuries from the remains of mud-brick towns, each layer burying the one before. Manzaratepa, near the town of Vose' in the Khatlon region, is one of these ancient settlement mounds, part of a network of sites in the fertile valleys between the Panj and Vakhsh rivers that were inhabited from the Bronze Age through the Kushan and early Islamic periods. Archaeological work has revealed traces of fortifications, houses and ceramics, and the sites are part of Tajikistan's long, rich and little-known history along the Silk Roads.

The landscape is a broad valley of cotton fields, orchards and villages, with the foothills of the Pamir rising to the east and the mountains of Afghanistan visible to the south on clear days. Summers are long and very hot, winters mild, and the irrigation canals that feed the fields have been dug and redug since ancient times. Kulob, the main city of the area, has a long history and the mausoleum of Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani, a fourteenth-century Sufi scholar from Persia.

For riders, Kulob is the gateway to the southern route of the Pamir Highway, which heads east from here toward Kalai-Khumb and follows the Panj river along the Afghan border, one of the great adventure roads of the world. The roads in Khatlon itself are mostly paved, with fast, straight stretches and some rough sections, potholes and unpredictable traffic, including livestock and slow-moving trucks. Police checkpoints are common, so keep your documents handy.

Vose', about five kilometres away, has fuel and basic shops, and Kulob, around twenty kilometres away, has a wider range of services. Fuel quality can be variable, so fill up at larger stations when you can. Food is simple and filling: plov, the rice dish with meat, carrots and onions, shashlik, grilled skewers, fresh bread and fruit from the orchards, especially melons and grapes in late summer.

April, May and October are the months to aim for. Summer heat can be extreme, often above forty degrees. Climb the mound for the view; pottery shards in the dust underfoot are a quiet reminder of just how long people have farmed this valley, and they belong exactly where they lie.
t.makbarai mavlono tojiddin@38.1,69.3:
Danghara is a small town in the Khatlon region of southern Tajikistan, best known in the country as the home town of the president, Emomali Rahmon, and the road to it is accordingly one of the better ones in the region. The town lies in a broad valley surrounded by low, bare hills, with fields of cotton and wheat watered by irrigation canals. The Makbarai Mavlono Tojiddin, a mausoleum near the town, is a local shrine, a place of pilgrimage and prayer that belongs to the long tradition of saints' tombs across Central Asia. It is among the sites linked to the Cultural Heritage of Ancient Khuttal, the medieval principality that once flourished in this region and that Tajikistan has proposed for UNESCO listing.

Khuttal was an important region in the early Islamic period, a crossroads on routes between Bactria, Sogdiana and the lands to the south, and its towns, fortresses and Buddhist and Islamic monuments are still being explored by archaeologists. Nearby, the ruins of Khishttepa, a Buddhist temple, and Shahrtepa, a fortified settlement, hint at the area's long and layered history. Visiting the mausoleum, dress modestly, remove your shoes where expected and be respectful of those praying.

The riding is a mix of good and challenging. From Dushanbe, the main road east and south crosses the Shar-Shar pass through a long tunnel and descends into the valleys of Khatlon. The road is generally well surfaced, but traffic can be heavy, with trucks and erratic driving, and livestock on the road is common. Nearby, the Nurek reservoir, held back by one of the highest dams in the world, offers stunning views of turquoise water among bare hills, and the road along its shore is a pleasure to ride.

The climate is continental, with very hot summers, when temperatures in the valleys can be extreme, and cold winters. Spring, when the hills are briefly green and covered in flowers, and autumn, when the harvest is in, are the best seasons.

Danghara, about four kilometres away, has fuel, shops and a bazaar; Norak and Dushanbe are larger centres. Fuel quality can vary, so fill up at major stations when you can. Tajik hospitality is legendary, and you may be invited for tea, bread and fruit by people you meet. Try plov, the rice dish with meat and carrots that is the centrepiece of every celebration, or qurutob, bread soaked in a sauce of dried yoghurt, topped with vegetables.
Panjakent sits in the upper Zeravshan valley in north-western Tajikistan, close to the border with Uzbekistan and Samarkand, and the valley has been a corridor for traders, armies and ideas since long before the Silk Road had a name. Near the village of Mazori Sharif, in the hills south of the river, stands the mausoleum of Khoja Muhammad Bashoro, built in the eleventh century, famous for its portal decorated with intricate carved terracotta, a fine example of early Islamic architecture in Central Asia. It remains a place of pilgrimage, and visitors should dress modestly and respect those who come to pray.

The valley is rich in history. Sarazm, a few kilometres west of Panjakent, is one of the oldest settlements in Central Asia, dating back to the fourth millennium BC, and was listed by UNESCO in 2010. Ancient Panjakent, on a terrace above the modern town, was a Sogdian city of the fifth to eighth centuries, whose houses were decorated with remarkable wall paintings, some of which are now in museums in Tajikistan and Russia. The Sogdians were the great merchants of the Silk Road, and their language served as a common tongue along the trade routes.

The landscape is dramatic: the Zeravshan river flows through a broad valley between the high Zeravshan and Turkestan ranges, with orchards and fields along the river and bare mountains above. South of Panjakent, the Haft Kul, or Seven Lakes, a string of turquoise lakes in the Fann mountains, are reached by a rough road through a narrow valley, a wonderful but demanding ride.

The main road from Dushanbe to Panjakent crosses the Fann mountains through the Anzob tunnel, which has a fearsome reputation for poor ventilation, water and potholes, and then follows the Zeravshan valley west. The roads are generally paved, but conditions vary, with rockfalls and landslides possible, especially in spring. Summer is the best time to ride, though temperatures can be very high in the valley.

Panjakent, around twenty-four kilometres away, has fuel, a bazaar, shops and guesthouses. Fill up whenever possible, and carry water. In the bazaar, look for dried fruits, nuts and fresh bread baked in tandoor ovens, and try a bowl of shurbo, a hearty meat and vegetable soup, or a plate of mantu, steamed dumplings. Tajik hospitality is warm and generous, and you may find yourself invited for tea by people you meet on the road.
t.shahrtepa@37.5,69.4:
Shahrtepa lies in the lowlands of southern Tajikistan, in Khatlon province, within sight of the Panj river and the Afghan hills beyond. The word tepa means a mound, and it is the right word: a mound that has built up over centuries as one settlement was layered over another, in the Bactrian country that Alexander crossed and that later fed the Kushan empire. A Buddhist temple site is linked with this area, a reminder that this was once a place where monks, merchants and caravans met on the way between India, Central Asia and China.

I do not want to claim more detail than I have, because the site is not widely documented and visits can be uncertain, so think of this as a stop in a landscape rather than a polished attraction. What you do see is the loess hills of the Khatlon region, dry and tawny in summer, bright green for a short spell in spring, with cotton fields, orchards, and villages of mud-brick houses. The Panj marks the border with Afghanistan, and you can see the opposite bank clearly, with farms and paths and sometimes people on the far shore, which is a sobering and quiet thing to watch.

Riding here is rough and rewarding for those who like it. Main roads are paved but patchy, with potholes that can appear without warning, and side roads quickly turn into dust or mud depending on the season. Traffic includes old Soviet-era lorries, donkey carts and the occasional herd of goats, so ride with caution. The border zone has checkpoints, and you should carry your passport and any required permits, and avoid photographing military installations. Spring and autumn are the pleasant seasons; summers are scorching, so start at dawn.

Farkhor, about seven kilometres away, is the nearest town and the place to get fuel, water and something to eat. Expect plov, the rice and meat dish served in big shared bowls, with flatbread and green tea, and you will usually be welcomed with more hospitality than you expected. Because fuel quality can vary, fill up in the larger towns when you can, and carry spare water.
t.tugay forests of the tigrovaya balka nat:
The Tigrovaya Balka, the Tiger Gully, lies in the far south of Tajikistan where the Vakhsh river runs down to meet the Panj and the Amu Darya, and it is an odd, lush corner in a dry country. The nature reserve protects tugay, the riverine forest of poplar, willow, tamarisk and wild olive that grows along the flood plains of Central Asian rivers, with thick reed beds and clearings of tall grass. It looks like a jungle, which is why it was called a gully of tigers. The Turan tiger, a relative of the Siberian tiger, lived here until the 1950s, when hunting and the clearing of reed land for cotton drove it to extinction.

What survives is rich in other wildlife. The Bukhara deer, or hangul, has been reintroduced here, and wild boar, golden jackals, jungle cats and pheasants live in the thickets, with big flocks of birds on the water in winter. The tugay forests are among the rarest ecosystems in the region, since most of them were cleared for farmland in the twentieth century, and the reserve is part of the wider effort to keep some of them.

The towns nearby, Shahritus and Dŭstí, are small, with shops and basic services, and the larger town of Kurgan-Tyube, also called Bokhtar, lies further north, with fuel, a bazaar and hotels. The area borders Afghanistan along the Panj, and a permit may be required for the border zone, so check with local authorities and travel companies before you go. The main road from Dushanbe south is paved but potholed, with trucks, donkeys and cotton wagons, and fuel is not always available, so carry extra.

Summers are very hot, regularly above forty degrees, with humidity near the river, so travel in spring or autumn. March and April are green and cool, with flowers on the plain, and October is warm and golden. Mosquitoes can be fierce near water. Eat plov, the rice dish cooked in a big cauldron, and drink green tea in a teahouse, and ask a local guide before you walk into the forest, because it is wild and the paths are unmarked.
Timur, the conqueror known in the West as Tamerlane, was born in 1336 in a village near Shakhrisyabz, and when he became ruler of an empire stretching from Delhi to Damascus, he spent heavily on his home town. He made it a showpiece, and the main monument was Ak-Saray, the White Palace, begun in 1380 and never completed in his lifetime. Only two piers of the entrance portal survive, but they rise about thirty-eight metres, covered in blue, turquoise and gold tilework, and they still dwarf everything around them, a statement of power so big that it is hard to photograph from close up.

The old centre has other buildings worth finding. The Kok Gumbaz mosque, built by Timur's grandson Ulugh Beg in 1435, has a ribbed blue dome, and the ensemble of Dorut Tilovat holds tombs, including the crypt Timur prepared for himself, though he ended up buried in Samarkand. UNESCO listed the historic centre in 2000, and the city's name, which means green city, comes from its gardens, orchards and apricots, melons and grapes.

Shakhrisyabz is a town of about fifty-seven thousand, with fuel, cafes and market stalls, and Kitab, to the south, is larger, with an astronomical observatory. In Uzbekistan, much of the traffic runs on compressed natural gas, and petrol can be scarce or unevenly available, so fill up whenever you see a station that sells it, and keep a spare. The best approach is the road from Samarkand over the Hissar mountains, through the Tashtakaracha pass, with long climbs, tight bends and views of snow peaks, and a surface that has been much improved, though trucks are slow on the grades.

The best months are April, May, September and October, when the days are warm and the nights cool. Summers are very hot, often beyond forty degrees. Eat samsa, baked pastries filled with lamb, and drink green tea in a shaded courtyard, and bring a hat, because the sun on the tiled portal is fierce in the afternoon.
Samarkand is one of those names that sounds invented, and then you arrive and find it is a real city with real traffic. It sits in the fertile valley of the Zeravshan river, with the Pamir-Alay foothills to the south and the Kyzylkum desert to the west, and it has been a crossroads since before Alexander the Great marched through in 329 BC. The old settlement of Afrasiab, on a plateau at the edge of town, was razed by Genghis Khan's army in 1220. Timur, who made the city his capital in the 1370s, rebuilt it on a far grander scale, filling it with the craftsmen, scholars and stonemasons he dragged back from every conquest.

The blue-tiled results are what the label means by Timurid. The Registan, a square framed by three madrasas, is the famous one, with the oldest, built for Ulugh Beg, dating from the 1420s. Ulugh Beg was Timur's grandson, and he was as much an astronomer as a ruler; the ruins of his observatory lie on a hill nearby, and his star catalogue stayed the standard for two centuries. Timur himself lies in the Gur-e-Amir mausoleum, under a dark slab of jade, below a ribbed turquoise dome. Further along, the Shah-i-Zinda is a lane of tombs climbing a hillside, each faced in ceramic of a slightly different blue. The European part of the label is the tree-lined Russian quarter built after 1868, when the tsar's army took the city, and its wide avenues feel like a different century.

Riding in is easy; riding around is a game of patience. The highway from Tashkent is fast and well surfaced, though it has plenty of trucks, sudden speed bumps and police who like to flag down foreigners. In the city, expect dense traffic, taxis that stop without warning and heat, which in July and August can push past forty degrees. Spring and autumn are the right seasons, with apricot blossom in April and clear skies in October.

Fuel is available in town, but Uzbekistan has had patchy supplies, and many cars run on gas, so fill up whenever you see a station that sells petrol and do not assume the next one will. For food, nothing beats the hot samsa from a tandoor and a plate of plov. The round, stamped bread of Samarkand is considered the best in the country, and the locals will tell you so.
t.the ensembles of abdi darun and ishrat k:
Samarkand is not just the Registan. On the rolling land just outside the city, there are quieter places where the Timurid age and earlier centuries left shrines that few visitors reach. The ensembles of Abdi Darun and Ishrat-khona are two of them. Abdi Darun is a pilgrimage complex linked to a revered holy man, with mosques, a gateway and a graveyard on a hillside above a stream, and for centuries local people have walked up here to pray and to picnic under the trees. Ishrat-khona, which means the House of Joy, is a ruined mausoleum from the fifteenth century, built for the women of the Timurid court, with a once splendid brick facade of turquoise tiles and carved terracotta.

The Timurid dynasty, descended from the conqueror Timur, who made Samarkand his capital in the late fourteenth century, was a great patron of architecture. Brick, glazed tile and gold were used in lavish quantities, and the domes seen across the city are the most famous legacy. At Ishrat-khona, the decoration is faded, and large parts of the building have fallen, but the arches and the shadows of tile work show how fine it once was. Samarkand's historic centre is on the World Heritage list, and these sites give a quieter, more intimate feel than the great monuments.

The roads around Samarkand are mostly wide and well surfaced, running through orchards, cotton fields and vineyards with the snowy peaks of the Zeravshan range on the horizon to the south. Traffic can be heavy in the city, with erratic drivers and little regard for lanes, and police checks are frequent. The best seasons are spring, when the orchards blossom and the hills are green, and autumn, when the grapes are ripe. Summer is very hot, regularly above forty degrees, and winters are cold, with snow.

Samarkand is a city of more than three hundred thousand people with plenty of fuel, though many vehicles run on gas, so check the station before you queue. Jomboy Shahri, ten kilometres away, is a smaller town. Take a taste of the local bread, baked in clay ovens and stamped with patterns, and of the sweet melons and dried fruit at the market. Dress modestly at the shrines, and take your shoes off where asked.
t.toksankoriz irrigation system@39.5,67.7:
Water is the oldest story in Central Asia, and the Zeravshan valley has told it for thousands of years. The river, whose name means gold-bearing, runs down from the glaciers of the Pamir-Alay in Tajikistan and into the desert of Uzbekistan, and every village along it lives by canals and underground channels. The word koriz, or kariz, is the local name for a qanat, a gently sloping tunnel that carries groundwater from the foothills to the fields, and the name Toksankoriz, as I read it, points to a system of many such channels. I cannot say more about the details of this site without risking error, but the principle is clear.

Panjakent, about eleven kilometres away, is the main town, a city of about thirty-five thousand people on the Zeravshan. Just outside it lie the ruins of ancient Panjakent, a Sogdian town of the fifth to eighth centuries, whose houses and temples were decorated with wall paintings of epics and gods, now in museums in Dushanbe and St Petersburg. The Sogdians were the great merchants of the Silk Road, who spoke an Iranian language and carried silk, silver and ideas from China to Persia. Nearby, the site of Sarazm, a town more than five thousand years old, is one of the oldest in Central Asia.

The mountains behind the town are the Fann range, a high, rugged group of peaks with turquoise lakes and glaciers, and the roads that climb into them are rough but beautiful. The main highway, running east towards Dushanbe, climbs over high passes and through long tunnels, with a surface that is improved in some stretches and damaged in others. Landslides, snow and ice can close sections, especially in spring and winter. The best period for travel is from late May to September.

Border formalities between Uzbekistan and Tajikistan have been changing in recent years, so check the current rules for crossing with a vehicle before you plan a route. Panjakent has fuel, shops and guesthouses, and the bazaar sells apricots, walnuts and flatbread. A cup of green tea and a plate of plov are the usual welcome.
t.shahristoni hulbuk@37.8,69.6:
Shahristoni is an old word for the inner town of a medieval city, and Hulbuk was a large one. In the ninth to eleventh centuries, when the Samanid dynasty ruled much of Central Asia from Bukhara, Hulbuk was the capital of Khuttal, a rich district in the south-east of what is now Tajikistan, and its rulers built a palace complex with courtyards, halls and fortified walls. Excavators have found fine carved alabaster panels, painted ceramics, glazed bowls and bits of mosaic, which show how sophisticated the court was, a Persian-speaking world that produced scholars, poets and astronomers. The city was destroyed in the Mongol invasion of the thirteenth century and never rebuilt.

The site lies in the Khatlon region, near the town of Vose, with about twenty thousand people, in a hot, dry landscape of low hills, irrigated fields and cotton, along the valley of the Yakhsu river, not far from the Panj river and the border with Afghanistan. Part of the palace has been restored, with new walls and a museum on the spot, and visitors can walk through reconstructed rooms. Outside, the remains of the old city show up as mounds and terraces in the grass.

Getting here is a journey in itself. From Dushanbe, the capital, roads go south and east via Kulob, a town with a long history and a mausoleum of the Sufi scholar Mir Sayid Ali Hamadani, and the roads are a mixed bag, with good asphalt, potholes, mountain passes and stretches of gravel. Fuel is available in Kulob and Vose, but quality can be poor, and distances between stations can be long, so carry a spare can. Traffic is light apart from lorries and the occasional donkey cart.

Summers are very hot, with temperatures above forty degrees, so spring, from April to June, and autumn are best. Winters are cold and snowy in the hills. Bring your passport, because police checkpoints are common and polite, and make sure your visa and registration are in order.

The local food is plov, rice cooked with meat and carrots, flat bread baked in clay ovens, melons in late summer and apricots and dried fruit. A guide helps, because signs are in Tajik and Russian.
t.castle on mount mugh@39.5,68.4:
The fortress of Mugh stands on a rocky hill above the Zeravshan valley in the mountains of northern Tajikistan, about twelve kilometres from Ayní. It looks like little today, a scatter of foundations and fallen mud-brick on a barren summit, but it holds one of the most important finds in Central Asian history. In 1932 a shepherd found a leather bag of old documents, and the manuscripts turned out to be letters, contracts and records written in Sogdian, the language of the merchants who ran the Silk Road across this region.

The man at the centre of the story is Dewashtich, a Sogdian ruler of Panjakent who refused to submit when Arab armies arrived in the early eighth century. He retreated to this mountain refuge, and his papers were hidden or abandoned when the fortress fell. He was captured and executed, and the documents lay under stones for twelve centuries. The collection includes a marriage contract, tax lists and letters, and it gives a detailed picture of daily life that no chronicle does.

The way here is a mountain journey. Coming from Dushanbe, the highway to the north climbs through the Fann range and past the Anzob tunnel, then drops toward the Zeravshan. Expect rough patches, potholes, rockfall and trucks grinding up the grades. The side roads toward the fortress are narrower and may need a sturdy bike and careful reading of the map. Late spring and early autumn are best. Winter snow can shut the passes and summer sun makes the open slopes oven-hot.

Ayní is a small place, and fuel is not guaranteed in the villages beyond it, so top up in Dushanbe or at the larger stations along the main highway and carry a small reserve. Tea and bread are available in roadside chaikhanas, which also make decent rest stops. The Zeravshan itself, milky with glacial melt, keeps you company for much of the way, and apricot orchards line the valley in spring.
t.dushanbe@38.6,68.8:
Dushanbe means Monday, and the name comes from a village market that took place on that day, long before the city arrived. Today Dushanbe is the capital of Tajikistan, a city of nearly seven hundred thousand people in a broad valley beneath the Gissar mountains, laid out on wide, tree-lined avenues with white marble buildings, fountains and parks, a Soviet creation with a distinctly Persian soul. The Tajik language is a form of Persian, and the poets of the region, Rudaki and Ferdowsi among them, are national heroes, whose statues stand in the city.

For motorcyclists, Dushanbe is the western end of the Pamir Highway, the legendary M41, which runs east through the mountains to Khorog, Murghab and on to Osh in Kyrgyzstan. Most riders spend a few days in the city to prepare. Fuel quality in the mountains is uncertain, so some riders carry extra, and spare parts and tyres are better sought here than anywhere on the road. The Tajik e-visa and the permit for the Gorno-Badakhshan region need to be arranged before leaving. Ask in the guesthouses and at the bike shops, where fellow travellers swap tips.

The riding out of the city is easy at first, with wide roads and light traffic. North of town, the Varzob gorge offers cool air, river views and weekend restaurants, and the long Anzob tunnel, which passes under the mountains, has been improved in recent years, though it can still be dark and wet. To the south, the road toward Kulob runs through cotton fields and hills before following the Panj river along the Afghan border. Expect potholes, trucks and goats.

Dushanbe has plenty of fuel stations, bazaars and cafés. Try plov, the rice and meat dish cooked in huge cauldrons, and sambusa pastries, with green tea. The Mehrgon bazaar and the central Green Bazaar sell nuts, dried fruit, melons and fresh bread.

Spring and autumn are the best seasons, because summers are hot and winters in the passes are brutal.
t.town of ancient penjikent@39.5,67.6:
On a dusty loess terrace just outside modern Panjakent, a few low mud ridges and pits are all that remain of one of the richest cities on the Silk Road. Fourteen centuries ago this was a Sogdian town of merchants, with two-storey houses, temples and walls covered in paintings of feasts, heroes and gods. The best frescoes went to the Hermitage in St Petersburg and to the Rudaki museum in town, so bring some imagination with you, but standing among the excavated streets with the Zeravshan glittering below, the scale of the place still lands.

The story ends badly, as Silk Road stories often do. When the Arab armies pushed into Sogdiana in the early eighth century, the ruler Devashtich fled up the valley to a fortress on Mount Mugh. Soviet archaeologists later found a cache of documents there, letters in Sogdian that gave historians a rare voice from inside a vanished culture. The poet Rudaki, often called the father of Persian poetry, is buried in a village a short ride up the hills, and locals will point you there with real pride.

The riding into Panjakent is the reason most travellers remember it. From Dushanbe you climb over the Fan range, through the long and notoriously grim Anzob tunnel, then follow the Zeravshan west through a gorge of grey and ochre cliffs, with apricot orchards wherever the valley widens. The surface varies from new Chinese-built asphalt to patches that will test your suspension, and lorries own the road on the climbs. To the west the border with Uzbekistan sits within a short hop, with Samarkand barely an hour beyond it, which makes this a natural start or finish for a loop between the two countries.

Panjakent itself is a proper market town of some thirty-five thousand people, so fuel, bread, melons and plov are easy to find, though octane quality can be uneven and many riders top up with care. The bazaar is the place for dried apricots, walnuts and green tea in a shady chaikhana. Mornings are cool even in summer; by afternoon the terrace bakes, so walk the ruins early, then ride up towards the Fan lakes for evening air and a cold glass of water from a mountain spring.
t.ajinatepa buddhist monastery@37.8,68.9:
In the Vakhsh valley of southern Tajikistan, near the city of Bokhtar, once called Qurghonteppa, a low mound of earth in the fields hides the remains of a Buddhist monastery from the seventh and eighth centuries. Excavations at Ajina Tepa, which means the hill of the demons in local tradition, revealed a complex of courtyards, cells, corridors and stupas, built of mud brick and decorated with paintings and clay sculptures. The most spectacular find, uncovered in 1966, was a giant reclining Buddha, around thirteen metres long, depicting the Buddha entering nirvana.

The Buddha was cut into pieces and moved to Dushanbe, where it is now displayed in the National Museum of Antiquities, the largest surviving Buddha statue in Central Asia. The monastery itself, today little more than eroded walls and mounds, belongs to the Silk Roads heritage that Tajikistan has put forward for UNESCO recognition, and its story reflects a time when Buddhism flourished along the trade routes linking India, China and Iran, before the arrival of Islam. Standing among the ruins, with cotton fields around and the mountains in the distance, it is hard to imagine the monks and pilgrims who once lived here.

Riding in southern Tajikistan is an experience in itself. The roads in the Vakhsh valley are mostly flat, with good asphalt on the main routes but potholes and rough patches on smaller roads. Old Soviet cars, trucks, donkey carts and cattle all share the tarmac, and police checkpoints are common. Further south, the Tigrovaya Balka nature reserve protects tugai forests along the Vakhsh and Panj rivers, home to rare animals, though access is restricted. Summers here are extremely hot, often over forty degrees, while spring and autumn are more comfortable.

Bokhtar, a city of tens of thousands, has fuel, shops, markets and restaurants. Fuel quality can vary, so fill up at reputable stations. Tajik food is hearty and generous: plov, rice cooked with meat, carrots and onions, is the national dish, and qurutob, bread soaked in a yoghurt sauce with vegetables, is a local favourite. Green tea is served everywhere, and hospitality is a matter of pride, so expect invitations to share a meal.
t.cultural heritage sites of ancient khutt:
Khuttal was a medieval kingdom in the south of what is now Tajikistan, centred on the fertile valleys between the Vakhsh and Panj rivers, and it flourished as a crossroads of trade and culture between Central Asia, Iran and India. The region's heritage includes the ruins of palaces, towns and religious buildings, such as the citadel of Hulbuk, near Vose', a royal residence from the ninth to the eleventh centuries, with richly decorated walls, and the town of Kulob, with the mausoleum of the fourteenth-century Sufi scholar Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani. Several of these sites have been nominated together for UNESCO recognition.

The landscape is a mix of irrigated valleys, cotton and wheat fields, and dry hills rising towards the mountains of the Pamir foothills. To the south, the Panj river forms the border with Afghanistan, and from some roads, you can see across the river to Afghan villages and fields. The region has a rich tradition of music, crafts and hospitality, and markets in towns like Kulob and Farkhor are full of colour, with fruit, vegetables, bread and textiles.

Riding here is an adventure. The main roads are mostly paved, but quality varies, and side roads can be rough and unpaved. You share the road with lorries, ageing Ladas, donkeys and wandering sheep, and the police stop vehicles often, particularly near the Afghan border, where permits may be required. Summers are very hot, often over forty degrees, and dust storms can occur, while winters are mild in the valleys but cold in the hills. The road along the Panj towards the Pamirs is one of the great adventure routes of Central Asia.

Farkhor, Vose' and Kulob have fuel, shops and restaurants, though fuel quality can vary. Tajik cuisine is generous: plov, shashlik, fresh bread baked in tandoor ovens, and sweet melons and grapes in summer. A pot of green tea arrives before you have even asked, and strangers may well insist you stay to eat. Respect local customs, dress modestly, and ask before photographing people, particularly women.
t.tali khamtuda fortress@39.4,67.9:
The Zeravshan valley in northwestern Tajikistan is one of the old arteries of Central Asia, a fertile ribbon of green squeezed between the Turkestan and Zeravshan ranges, and in the hills above it lie the ruins of fortresses that once guarded the eastern approaches to Sogdiana. Tali Khamtuda is one of these, and nearby stands the castle on Mount Mugh, where one of the most dramatic stories of the region took place. In 722 Devashtich, the ruler of Panjakent, fled here with his people from the advancing Arab armies, and after a siege he surrendered and was executed. In 1933 a shepherd found a basket of documents in the ruins, written on leather, paper and wood in the Sogdian language, which turned out to be Devashtich's archive and one of the most important sources for understanding Sogdian society.

Panjakent, about twenty-five kilometres to the west, is the modern town that grew beside the ruins of ancient Panjakent, a Sogdian city of merchants, temples and wall paintings, sometimes called the Pompeii of Central Asia. Its frescoes are now in museums, some in Dushanbe and some in the Hermitage in St Petersburg, but the excavated city on its plateau above the river is evocative. Samarkand, across the border in Uzbekistan, is only about sixty kilometres to the west.

The road up the Zeravshan from Panjakent towards Ayni follows the river through a deepening valley, with villages, apricot orchards and walnut trees on the terraces and big mountains rising on both sides. The surface is mostly paved but rough in places, with rockfall, washouts and livestock to watch for. From Ayni, the road to Dushanbe climbs to the Anzob tunnel, notorious among riders for its darkness, water, potholes and fumes. Side valleys lead to the Fann Mountains and the Haft Kul, the Seven Lakes, a string of turquoise lakes along a dramatic valley.

Panjakent has fuel stations, a bazaar and simple restaurants; in the mountains, fuel is scarce and quality varies. Carry spare fuel and water, and a good map. Food is simple: plov, non bread, lagman noodles and green tea, served with generous hospitality. Summer brings heat in the valley and cool nights in the mountains; winter closes many high roads.
t.zoli zard@38.1,69.3:
Danghara lies in the south of Tajikistan, in the province of Khatlon, on the broad, hot plain between the Hissar mountains and the Panj river, which forms the border with Afghanistan. The point called Zoli Zard sits just outside the town, and the name, which means yellow water in Persian, probably refers to a stream or spring in the loess hills. Shahristoni Zoli Zar, as the other ride calls it, suggests an old fortified town site, the kind of mound that dots this part of Central Asia, though I cannot tell you exactly what was found there. The region is full of such sites, and many of them belong to the long Buddhist, Zoroastrian and later Islamic history of Bactria.

One of the best known, not far to the west, is Ajina-Tepa, a Buddhist monastery of the seventh and eighth centuries, where archaeologists found a huge clay reclining Buddha about twelve metres long, now in the national museum in Dushanbe. It shows how far Buddhism had spread along the Silk Road before the Arab conquest. The land has seen Greeks under the successors of Alexander, the Kushans, the Hephthalites and Turks pass through, and each has left a layer in the soil.

For a rider, the roads in this part of Tajikistan can be good, bad or non-existent, sometimes in the same kilometre. The main route from Dushanbe passes by the Nurek reservoir, formed by one of the highest dams in the world, built in the Soviet era, with a road that winds along the cliffs above the turquoise water. The plains are hot and dusty in summer, with temperatures above forty degrees, so spring and autumn are better. Cotton fields, melon stalls and clay-walled villages line the way, and police checkpoints are common, so keep your papers handy. The border zone near Afghanistan has its own rules, so ask about permits before leaving the main roads.

Danghara, a town of nearly twenty-three thousand, has fuel, a market and simple restaurants where plov, the rice and meat dish cooked in a huge pot, is the standard meal. Norak, the town by the Nurek dam, is the other major stop. Drink bottled water, carry spare fuel for the longer sections and be patient with delays, which are an ordinary part of travelling in Tajikistan. The hospitality of people in the villages is generous, and a pot of green tea is always offered.
t.sanjarshakh settlement@39.5,67.7:
Sanjarshakh lies in the Zarafshan valley of Tajikistan, a short ride from the town of Panjakent, and its low mounds and walls are the remains of a Sogdian settlement. The Sogdians were the great merchants of Central Asia, who spoke an Iranian language and carried silk, spices, paper and ideas along the Silk Road from China to Persia and beyond, and their language was the common tongue of the trade routes for several centuries. Their towns lay in the valleys of the Zarafshan and the Kashkadarya, and Panjakent, a few kilometres from here, is the best known, with houses decorated with wall paintings of epic stories, banquets and gods, that are now in the Hermitage in Saint Petersburg.

The Arab conquest in the early eighth century changed the region. The last Sogdian ruler, Divashtich, held out in a mountain fortress at Mount Mug in the Zarafshan valley and was defeated around 722, and Sogdian culture slowly faded, though the people and the language left their mark on the later Persian culture of the region. The poet Rudaki, regarded as the father of Persian poetry, was born in a village near Panjakent in the ninth century.

The setting is wonderful. Panjakent lies at the foot of the Fann mountains, a spectacular range of snow peaks and turquoise lakes, with the Zarafshan river rushing down through its valley and orchards of apricots, apples and walnuts around the villages. The road from Dushanbe crosses a high mountain pass, partly through a long tunnel, and the road conditions have changed over the years, so ask locally about the current state before setting out. On the Panjakent side, the road is a pleasure, with a good deal of traffic from trucks and shared taxis.

Panjakent, a town of over thirty-five thousand, has fuel stations, a lively bazaar and simple guest houses, and it is the starting point for trips to the Seven Lakes at Marguzor and Iskanderkul. Summer is hot in the valley but cool in the mountains, and the high passes are blocked by snow from late autumn to late spring. Buy bread, apricots and almonds at the bazaar, and enjoy a bowl of shorba, soup with lamb and vegetables, in one of the small cafes.
t.kalai hulbuk@37.8,69.6:
Hulbuk was the capital of a small principality of the Samanid era in what is now southern Tajikistan, and it is one of the most evocative ruins in the Khatlon region. Its location is on the plains south of Vose, near the Kyzylsu, within sight of the Afghan border country. Archaeologists dug out a palace complex of mud-brick and fired brick from the ninth to eleventh centuries, with remarkable carved terracotta panels and a ceramic tradition that left glazed bowls with sharp, graceful script. Some of this is displayed in a small museum on site, and part of the citadel has been reconstructed so you can see how the high rooms were arranged.

What you will notice first is the scale of the mound, rising from flat cultivated land, and the silence around it. The Khatlon plains are warm and dry, with cotton fields, poplar windbreaks, and herds of sheep being walked along canals. In spring the hills behind are green and carry wildflowers, and by July the ground goes pale and cracked.

Riding here is an adventure of a different sort from the Pamir Highway. Roads between Kŭlob, Vose and the villages are paved but unevenly, with sections of broken asphalt, patches, and potholes that can be deep. Livestock, donkey carts, and overloaded cars move at their own pace, and drivers overtake with optimism. It is not a place for night riding. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, because summers are very hot and winter sometimes brings snow and ice on the hills toward Kŭlob.

Vose, about eight kilometres away, is a town of more than twenty thousand people and the logical place to find fuel, bread, tea and a simple meal. Kŭlob, about twenty-five kilometres off, is larger and has more services. Fuel quality can be variable in Tajikistan, so top up where you see a busy pump, and carry extra if you head into the countryside. Locals are curious and generous, and an invitation to tea is more likely than not, so leave a little time in the day. Ask permission before you photograph people, and keep to the paths on the mound, since the walls are fragile.
t.kum settlement@39.4,68.4:
The Zeravshan is the river that waters Samarkand and Bukhara far downstream, and up here in its upper valley it is a cold, hurrying thing between steep walls of the Zeravshan and Hissar ranges. The Kum area lies on the way between Ayní and the Fan Mountains, in Tajikistan's Sughd region, and it belongs to the Sogdian world, the merchant culture that carried silk, glass, paper and ideas along the old routes between China and Persia. Settlement mounds and fortress sites dot the valley, some of them partly worn away by farming and floods, and the area holds a few of the most famous finds of Sogdian history, among them the archives of letters and contracts found in the twentieth century on a nearby mountain.

On the ground you will see earthen mounds and old walls that are easy to mistake for natural hills, with apricot orchards and cornfields at their feet. There is not much signposting and no ticket office. The interest lies in the setting, the way a ruined fort commands a side valley, the way the river bends below, the way the light turns orange at the end of the day against the red slopes.

The road from Dushanbe to Ayní passes over the Anzob Pass, or goes through the long tunnel beneath it, and then follows the Zeravshan downstream. This is real mountain riding, with long climbs, steep drops, and a surface that varies from good tarmac to broken edge and gravel patches, with rockfalls and landslides after storms. The tunnel has had a poor reputation for ventilation and lighting, so be prepared. Early summer and early autumn are the best seasons. In spring, snowmelt raises the river and mud slides can close sections, and in winter the pass is serious.

Ayní, about thirteen kilometres away, is only a small town, but it is the main halt in the upper valley, with a market, a few shops and tea houses, and basic fuel from roadside sellers, which is not always dependable, so fill up in Dushanbe or Penjikent whenever you can. Locals are open and curious, and a pot of green tea with bread and apricots is the usual welcome. Carry water, spare tubes, and warm layers, since evenings are cool at this altitude.
t.afrosiab archaeological area@39.7,67.0:
Samarkand as the Mongols found it lay not where the tourists now go but on a high, dusty plateau north of the modern town. That plateau is Afrosiab, the old city, and it was already ancient when Alexander the Great took it in 329 BC under the name Marakanda. It flourished as a Sogdian capital, saw Arab armies arrive in the eighth century, and kept growing until 1220, when Genghis Khan swept in and destroyed it so thoroughly that it was never rebuilt. The survivors drifted south, and Timur later raised his capital on the new ground.

What remains is a landscape of low hills, trenches and eroded walls, over two hundred hectares of mud-brick ruin with the cemetery of Shah-i-Zinda along its southern edge. It is hard to read at first, but the small museum on site makes the effort worthwhile. Its pride is a set of seventh-century wall paintings from a Sogdian palace, showing ambassadors bringing gifts to the local king, with Chinese, Turkic and Korean-looking figures among them, a vivid picture of how far people travelled. Photographs are usually permitted for a small fee.

Riding in is easy. Samarkand's main roads are wide, the surface is mostly good, and traffic is dense but polite by regional standards. On the outskirts the highways to Tashkent, Bukhara and Penjikent are well paved, with some potholes, and heavy lorries, so keep your wits about you when overtaking. The best seasons are spring and autumn, when the city is green or golden and the heat is moderate. July and August are very hot, and winter days can be cold and grey, with a bit of snow.

Everything you need is close, since Samarkand has more than three hundred thousand people. Near the Registan, tea houses serve plov, samsa baked in clay ovens, and flatbread stamped with patterns. The Afrosiab site is open daily, with a ticket and cash being the safest option, and the afternoon is best for the low sun on the ruins.
Samarkand is one of those cities that leaves you fumbling for comparisons. It sits in the Zeravshan valley in eastern Uzbekistan, with the snow-capped Turkestan range on the horizon, and for the last two thousand years or so it has been a crossroads of peoples. The part visited today is largely Timur's, from the late fourteenth century, when the conqueror brought in craftsmen from Persia, India, Syria and the Caucasus to make his capital the most splendid place in the world. Under his grandson Ulugh Beg the city also became a centre of science.

What stays in the mind is colour. The Registan, a square framed by three madrasas, glows with blue and turquoise tiles and gold lettering. The Gur-e-Amir mausoleum, where Timur lies beneath a slab of dark green jade, has a ribbed blue dome that looks too big for its drum. The Bibi-Khanym mosque was meant to be the largest in the Islamic world, and part of it collapsed almost as soon as it was finished. Shah-i-Zinda, a street of tombs in glazed tile, seems to shift from one blue to another as you climb the stairs. Spend a morning there before the groups arrive.

Riding in Samarkand is city riding, with wide boulevards, roundabouts, a good many taxis and a few traffic police who like to stop foreigners, so keep your papers handy and ride calmly. Parking beside the sights is usually easy, though the Registan area has restrictions. In the countryside around the city the roads head into the foothills toward Urgut and Penjikent, and from there the real bends begin. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, because summer is intensely hot and winter can bring cold fog.

The services in town are excellent, with markets, bakeries and guesthouses of every kind, and a lively old bazaar by the Bibi-Khanym where you can buy dried apricots, nuts and warm round bread, the Samarkand style with its bright stamped patterns. Carry small notes of som, since cards are not universal, and treat evening as the best hour, when the lights come on the tile and the heat has gone.
t.ulugh bek s observatory@39.7,67.0:
Ulugh Beg was a strange kind of ruler. He was Timur's grandson, governor of Samarkand and then the whole realm, but his heart lay with the stars, and around 1420 he built an observatory on a hill north-east of the city that was among the finest in the world. The principal instrument was a gigantic meridian arc, a curved track set into a trench, with a radius of some forty metres, which let his astronomers measure the positions of stars with remarkable accuracy. The star catalogue they compiled, the Zij-i-Sultani, stayed a standard reference for over two centuries, and it corrected many errors in Ptolemy's.

The building itself was destroyed after Ulugh Beg was killed in 1449, probably on the orders of his own son, since religious conservatives resented a scientist king. It vanished from sight until a Russian archaeologist, Vasily Vyatkin, located the buried arc in 1908. What you see today is the lower portion of the great sextant, two curving marble-lined tracks descending into the earth, which you can walk beside. A small museum nearby holds copies of the star charts, instruments and portraits.

The ride up is a short one from the centre, along streets that climb gently to the hilltop of Chupan-Ata. Tarmac is good, traffic moderate, and there is parking by the museum. It is not a ride in the sporting sense, but the view of the city and the Zeravshan plain is lovely, particularly on a clear late afternoon when the Turkestan range shows its snow. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, while summer middays can bake the hilltop.

Samarkand has everything you need, from fuel stations to restaurants. The tea houses nearby serve plov and strong green tea, and in the old town you will find round bread and sweets. The site charges a modest entry fee and keeps limited hours, so check before you go, and bring a hat, since there is little shade on the hill.
t.namazgoh mosque@39.6,67.0:
Many Central Asian cities used to keep a namazgoh, an open prayer ground just outside the walls, where the whole male population gathered for the great feast days, in rows on the bare earth, led by an imam at a niche in a wall. The one at Samarkand lies on the southern fringe of the old town, a little way from the dense maze of lanes around the Registan, and it tells the story of how the city lived rather than how its rulers showed off. The structure, with its niche, a screen of arches and later additions, has been repaired and rebuilt over the centuries, so it is best seen as a layered place rather than a single period piece.

The ordinary character of the spot is part of its charm. Neighbourhood life goes on around it, with children in school uniforms, old men on benches, and families walking to a nearby market. Women's visits are usually restricted around prayer times, and everyone should dress modestly, with covered arms and legs, and leave shoes at the door when entering any prayer space. There is little signage, so a little local knowledge helps.

The riding is urban. Samarkand's streets here are a mix of broad avenues and narrow residential lanes, with taxis, buses, bicycles and the odd donkey cart. The surfaces are mostly decent, though ruts and manholes can surprise you, and drivers are accustomed to improvising. Early morning is the best time, when the light is gentle and the streets are quiet. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, while summer afternoons are blazing and winters are chilly.

You are close to everything in the city, with fuel stations on the main roads, supermarkets, bakeries and tea houses within a few minutes, and the Registan about two to three kilometres away. The bazaar nearby is the place to try warm non bread, dried fruit, and sweet halva, and tea houses serve plov at lunch. Many Uzbek cars run on compressed gas, so petrol pumps are less common than you would expect, and it pays to top up when you see one. Keep small notes for tipping and market buying, and be prepared to be greeted warmly, for the curiosity about foreign riders is considerable.
t.gardani khisor settlement@39.4,68.3:
Khisor, or Hissar, is a word that turns up across Central Asia for a fortress, and Gardani Khisor is one of those lonely fortress-hills of the upper Zeravshan valley in Tajikistan. It stands a few kilometres from the river, west of the little town of Ayní, in country where the plain narrows and the Fan Mountains start to rear up to the south. I can tell you the setting better than the ruin, because there is not much published on the site and what stands is mostly broken walls and mounds, but the pattern is familiar. The Sogdians and their successors put small forts on rocky knolls to watch the river road and the side valleys, and the villagers below kept orchards and flocks within shouting distance of safety.

Take a look at what sits around the fort. Terraced fields climb the slopes, walnut and apricot trees shade the lanes, and the air smells of dust, wood smoke and crushed thyme when the wind turns. Snow lingers on the high peaks into early summer, while down in the valley the afternoons can be properly hot. Birdwatchers will find wheatears, choughs and the occasional eagle riding the thermals along the rock faces.

The riding here is mountain work, and it asks for patience. Between Dushanbe and Ayní you either cross the Anzob Pass or run through its long tunnel, and beyond that the road along the Zeravshan alternates between decent asphalt and a patchwork of repairs, loose stone after rain, and the occasional rockfall. Trucks grind along in low gear, and cows and goats treat the road as shared pasture. The best months are late May to June and again in September and October. Spring floods can undermine the bank, and winter is a different story entirely.

Ayní, about seventeen kilometres from here, is the nearest place with a market, tea houses and informal fuel stalls, but supply in this part of the country is unreliable, so fill your tank in Dushanbe or Penjikent and carry a can. Drinking water from the villages is generally safe only if boiled or treated, so bring a filter or tablets. Hospitality is a strong tradition, and refusing the tea and flatbread that are offered at a village gate is a hard thing to do gracefully, so build a margin into the day.
t.khishttepa buddhist temple@38.3,69.9:
In the south of Tajikistan, in the hot valleys of Khatlon that lead toward the Afghan border, a mound of clay brick holds the ruins of a Buddhist monastery. Khishttepa, near the town of Mu'minobod, was a monastic complex in the early Middle Ages, probably in the seventh and eighth centuries, when Buddhism still flourished in the lands along the Amu Darya, or Oxus, the river that now marks the border. The remains include walls of mud brick, vaulted rooms and, in their day, painted walls and clay statues, of which only traces survive. Central Asia was a place where Buddhism, Zoroastrianism and later Islam met, and the monasteries of Bactria, as this region was called, sent monks and ideas along the Silk Road to China.

The landscape is dry and hilly, golden in summer, with loess hills, terraced fields of wheat, cotton and sunflowers, and small villages of mud-brick houses with flat roofs, backed by the snowy peaks of the Pamir foothills on a clear day. The mountains are steep and eroded, and the valleys are cut by rivers that run brown with silt in spring. The summers are fierce, with temperatures over forty degrees, so the best months for a visit are April, May, September and October.

Tajik roads can be demanding. The main routes between towns are paved but often patched, with potholes, and the side roads to villages and ruins are gravel or earth, which turns to slick mud in the rain. Livestock, donkeys and children use the road freely, and trucks and old Soviet-era vehicles move slowly. This is also a border zone, so expect checkpoints, carry your passport and registration documents at all times, and ask locally about restricted areas, since some places near the frontier require special permits. The ride goes on to Shahrtepa, another ancient site, through the same landscape.

Mu'minobod is a small town of about twelve thousand people, twenty-five kilometres away, with limited facilities, and the nearest big place for fuel, a good meal and a bed is Kulob, a larger city to the north. Fuel quality can vary, so fill up when you can, and carry water and some food. In the villages, hospitality is warm, and you may be invited for tea, with bread, dried fruit and sweets laid out on a cloth. A few words of Tajik or Russian go a long way, and so does a smile.
t.tohir caravansarai@37.7,69.3:
A caravanserai is the original motorway service station, and the one at Tohir shows how much trouble medieval travellers took to rest. These fortified inns stood at intervals along the trade routes of Asia, a day's journey apart, with a gate big enough for a laden camel, an open court for the animals and rooms for merchants and their goods, so that a caravan could stop safely at the end of a day. Tohir lies in the south of Tajikistan, in the hot valley of the Panj river, which forms the border with Afghanistan, and the tracks that passed it probably linked the Oxus crossings and the old cities of Bactria to the mountain valleys of the north. The place has the hushed look of a ruin in a farm landscape, with clay brick walls and arched openings catching the afternoon sun.

The landscape is that of south Tajikistan: hot, dry hills of loess, patches of cotton and wheat in the valleys, mud-brick villages with flat roofs, and a long wall of mountains on the horizon. Farkhor, the town some twenty-nine kilometres away, is close to the border, and the Panj is wide and brown here, with Afghan villages visible on the far bank. It is an extraordinary thing to look across the water at a different country, with donkeys and men on motorbikes going about their business on the other side.

Riding here requires care and preparation. The area is a border zone, with checkpoints, so carry your passport, visa and registration documents, and ask local officials or your host about permits and restricted areas before you travel. The roads are paved on the main routes, but patched, with potholes, and the side roads are gravel or dirt. In summer, the heat is intense, over forty degrees, so start early and drink plenty of water, and in winter, the days are cool and clear. The ride continues to Shahrtepa through villages and fields.

Farkhor has fuel and basic shops, but the choices are limited, and fuel quality varies, so fill up when you can and carry some extra. Dushanbe, the capital, to the north, has a much wider range of services. In the villages, tea and bread are offered freely, and the hospitality is generous. Learn a few words of Tajik, or Russian, and be respectful, particularly of women and of religious customs, as this is a conservative region.
t.samarkand@39.7,67.0:
Samarkand is one of the oldest cities in Central Asia, and a name that has meant romance to travellers for two and a half thousand years. It sits in the green valley of the Zeravshan River, with the Pamir-Alay mountains rising to the south, on the great trade route that carried silk, paper, spices and ideas between China and the Mediterranean. Alexander the Great took the city, then called Marakanda, in 329 BC, and the mound of its ancient site, Afrasiab, still lies on the northern edge of the modern town. The paper trade is said to have reached the Islamic world here in the eighth century, when Chinese prisoners taught the craft after a battle on the Talas River.

What you see today, though, is mostly the work of Timur, the conqueror known in the West as Tamerlane, who made Samarkand his capital in the late fourteenth century and filled it with craftsmen seized from the lands he conquered. The Registan, a great square framed by three madrasas faced in blue, turquoise and gold tilework, was built over two centuries, with the earliest, the madrasa of Ulugh Beg, dating from the 1420s. Ulugh Beg, Timur's grandson, was an astronomer-king, and the ruins of his observatory, with a giant underground sextant, lie on a hill outside town. His star catalogue was the finest of its age.

Other sights are almost as good. The Gur-e-Amir, the mausoleum where Timur is buried, has a ribbed turquoise dome and a dark jade slab over his tomb. The Shah-i-Zinda, a lane of tombs climbing a hillside, is a dazzling run of blue tile that is among the most beautiful places in the Islamic world, and the Bibi-Khanym mosque, huge and partly ruined, speaks of Timur's ambitions. Samarkand's bread, round, thick and stamped with patterns, is sold in the Siyob bazaar and is superb with the local grapes and melons.

For riders, the city is the start of the road west toward Bukhara, around 270 kilometres across a flat plain on a well-used highway. Traffic in the city is chaotic, and driving habits are hard to predict, so ride defensively. Summers are very hot, often above forty degrees, and the best seasons are spring and autumn. Fuel can be unpredictable in Uzbekistan, since many vehicles run on gas and supplies of higher-octane petrol are not always reliable, so top up whenever you see a working station and carry a little extra if you can. A city of over three hundred thousand people has plenty of hotels and restaurants, and plov, the local rice and lamb dish, is the thing to order.
t.novo hamburgo@-29.7,-51.1:
Novo Hamburgo is where the Rota Romântica begins, and it begins with leather. This is a city of a quarter of a million people on the Rio dos Sinos, about forty kilometres north of Porto Alegre in Rio Grande do Sul, and for most of the twentieth century it made a large share of Brazil's shoes. Factories, tanneries and outlet stores still line the main roads, and the city carries its nickname, capital of footwear, without any embarrassment. It is the commercial end of a German-speaking colonisation story that started in the 1820s.

The first German settlers in the state arrived in 1824 at nearby São Leopoldo, and the valley of the Sinos river filled up with farmers, craftsmen and tradespeople from the Rhineland and Hunsrück, who brought half-timbered houses, Lutheran and Catholic churches, choirs and a fondness for sausage and cake. Novo Hamburgo split from São Leopoldo much later, in the 1920s, and its historic neighbourhood of Hamburgo Velho still keeps old buildings, a museum and quiet streets under big trees. The German heritage is thinner here than in the hills, though, and the best of it is found as you climb away from the city.

For a rider, this is a gateway rather than a destination. The first kilometres out of town are urban, with traffic lights, trucks and the heavy tempo of an industrial region, and the real road starts after you leave the valley floor. Before that, treat it as a practical stop. It has fuel stations at every junction, workshops, supermarkets and a wide choice of lunch places, from self-service buffets where you pay by weight to churrascarias serving grilled meat in endless rounds. Be careful with your things in the busy centre, as you would in any Brazilian city of this size.

The countryside beyond is the Serra Gaúcha, where roads wind up from the plain through eucalyptus plantations and araucaria pines toward Nova Petrópolis and Gramado. The air cools as you gain height, the light turns clearer, and the little towns have names that sound like Bavaria. In winter, mornings can be cold and foggy even down here, and frost is not unknown on the higher roads.

The best days are in autumn and spring, when it is neither stifling nor wet. Summer heat and thunderstorms are common, with intense afternoon downpours, so an early start is wise. Plan to leave the city before the afternoon traffic, and take a waterproof layer, even if the morning looks bright.
t.nova petropolis@-29.4,-51.1:
Nova Petrópolis is the German town that grew into a garden. It sits in the Serra Gaúcha, on the plateau above the river valleys of Rio Grande do Sul, and its streets, squares and hedges are kept with a fussiness that would impress a Bavarian council. The town was founded in the 1850s by German immigrants, and its identity is still bound up with that history, with half-timbered buildings, choirs, folk dance groups and menus that arrive with sauerkraut, sausages and thick cakes.

The most famous of the town's gardens is the Labirinto Verde, a hedge maze laid out in a pattern of walls and corridors, and a pleasing place to waste an hour. The Praça das Flores in the centre is a plant-filled square with trees, flowerbeds and a view of the church. Nearby, the Parque Aldeia do Imigrante is a village of reconstructed early houses, showing how the settlers lived, with old tools and costumes. The town also hosts an international choir festival, and in the evening you may hear voices drifting from a church, because singing is an important part of local life.

A piece of history here goes beyond the pretty gardens: in 1902, a Jesuit priest, Theodor Amstad, helped found the first credit cooperative in Brazil in the district of Linha Imperial, and the town still describes itself as the cradle of Brazilian cooperatives. The idea was simple, that poor farmers could pool their savings and lend to each other, and it spread across the country and grew into a large financial network. It is an unusual claim to fame, and the town is proud of it.

The riding on the Rota Romântica between Nova Petrópolis and Gramado is a relaxed run through hills, with pines, hydrangea hedges and gentle bends. The surface is generally good, with some patches, and traffic can thicken on weekends and holidays, when visitors flood in from Porto Alegre. Morning fog is common in the cooler months, and rain showers sweep in quickly, so a layer is useful. The scenery is mostly small farms, plantations and orchards, with flowers along the verges in spring.

Nova Petrópolis is large enough to have fuel stations, cafes and supermarkets, so there is no problem in stopping. For food, look for a café colonial, the traditional spread of breads, cakes, cold cuts, jams and coffee that is served in the afternoon. Try the cuca, a German-style crumb cake, and buy a jar of local honey or jam to take with you.
t.gramado@-29.4,-50.9:
Gramado is a mountain town that has been styled, with great confidence, as a fairy-tale village, and it works. Chalet-style houses with steep roofs, window boxes of flowers, chocolate shops, fondue restaurants and neat gardens fill the centre, and the cool air at around eight hundred metres, so different from the heat of the coast, makes the whole thing feel more convincing. The hydrangeas that line the streets bloom in summer, and in winter the town sometimes has frost and, once in a while, a dusting of snow.

The town grew from a modest settlement of German and Italian farmers in the Serra Gaúcha, and became a tourist destination in the twentieth century, when Brazilians from the hot lowlands began to come up for the climate. It now hosts two big events: a film festival, held each August since 1973, which showcases Brazilian and Latin American cinema, and the Natal Luz, a long Christmas season with parades, lights and shows that draws a large crowd. At those times the streets are busy to the point of gridlock, and hotels are full months ahead.

Beside Gramado lies Canela, a slightly larger and less polished town, known for its stone cathedral and for the Caracol waterfall, which drops more than a hundred metres in a single plume in the middle of a forest park. The Black Lake, a small artificial lake in Gramado ringed by trees and with swan-shaped paddle boats, is a favourite stop, and the shops on the main street sell chocolates, knitwear and leather goods. It is pleasant, if commercial, and the quality of the chocolate is surprisingly high.

For riders, the road is the point.
